script.text: Monday, April 7
My alarm goes off at 5:40.
I'm usually awake before it. I lie there for the full ten seconds anyway, as a matter of principle, listening to the house.
The water heater ticking. A crow on the power line. Nothing from downstairs.
Second year of high school starts today. It doesn't feel like anything starts. It feels like Monday.
I get up.

The rice was on the timer last night, so the kitchen already smells like steam. Eggs, the leftover spinach, the last of the frozen {karaage|fried chicken}. Two lunch boxes, side by side on the counter.
I've gotten fast at this. Fast enough to do it while reading the whiteboard on the fridge.
Kendo: Monday, Wednesday, Friday and Saturday morning. Hoshino Kitchen: Tuesday, Thursday and Sunday. A red circle around the 18, Akane's clinic day. All of it in my handwriting.
All of it except the bottom line, which still says "Garbage: burnables, Mon/Thu" in Dad's. He wrote it last spring. I've never written over it.
The {fusuma|sliding door} to Mom's room is closed. It usually is.
"Morning, Onii-chan…"
My sister shuffles in already dressed for school, eyes still at half-mast.
"Morning. How'd you sleep?"
"Geez, Onii-chan! Every single morning!"
"And?"
"And I slept! Super well! I didn't wake up once!"
I look at her anyway. Color's fine. She isn't leaning on the doorframe. She isn't holding her head the way she does when the room starts tilting on her.
"Onii-chan, you're hovering again."
"I'm standing in my own kitchen."
"Then go hover over the eggs!"
"There's an egg with your name on it."
"Yaaay. …I could make my own lunch, you know."
"I'm already making two."
"…You always are."
She says it to the rice cooker, not to me. I pretend I didn't hear that.
The back door slides open. No knock. There's never a knock.
"Good morning. I'm coming in."
"You're already in."
"Then I've arrived. Good morning, Akane-chan."
"Morning, Nanoha-chan!"
She sets a plastic container on the table.
"{Kinpira|braised burdock}. Mom made too much again."
"Again."
"Again. She can't measure burdock. It's a sickness."
She's been bringing food over for about a year now. I used to argue. Somewhere around last summer, I gave up.
"Tell her thanks."

She goes to the cupboard left of the sink, the one with the mugs and not the one with the glasses, and takes down two without looking. She bumps the drawer under the counter with her hip so it won't stick. She reaches over the sink and jiggles the window latch at the exact angle it needs, so the steam can get out.
She's been doing all of that since she was tall enough to reach.
Which, considering it's Nanoha, wasn't that long ago.
"I heard that."
"I didn't say anything."
"You thought it in a short-person direction."
"He totally did."
"Traitor."
"Nanoha-chan brought {kinpira||kinpira}!"
I wrap the lunches. I knock twice on the {fusuma||fusuma}.
"Mom, we're heading out. There's rice in the cooker and miso soup on the stove. Just heat it up."
Nothing.
Then a small shift of weight on the other side of the paper. A creak of floorboard.
That's an answer. Sort of.
The path to school follows the river for a while before it turns toward town.

This week it's the best walk in Shirasawa. The cherry trees along the embankment are in full bloom, so heavy with flowers the branches sag over the path, and every time the wind comes down off the mountains the whole tunnel lets go at once.

Up on the hill above it all, where the shrine is, the Ōzakura is blooming too: one cherry tree older than anyone's records, so big that from the bridge it looks like a pink cloud caught on the hillside.
Nanoha walks on the river side.
"Now then. Class assignments."
"They'll be posted at the entrance."
"That's the boring answer. I've prepared a theory."
"Of course you have."
"There are six second-year classes. On paper, our odds of being in the same one are one in six."
"But we've been in the same class four years running. At this point it's not luck. It's paperwork."
"Paperwork."
"A folder in the staff room. Both our names on the front. 'Do not separate,' underlined twice."
"Why would the staff room care?"
"Safety. If they split us up, I'd have to make new friends. Nobody wants that."
"Least of all the new friends."
"You have friends."
"I have Rika-chan. Rika-chan counts as several."
I laugh.
"You laughed. That's two points for me this morning."
"We're keeping score now?"
"We've always been keeping score. You're losing."
A gust shakes the trees. Petals come down all at once, thick enough to lose the path in. One lands on her braid.
I don't mention it. It suits her.
"Kō-chan. Your collar."
Before I can do anything about it, she's in front of me, folding my shirt collar back down over my tie.
Her hands stay a second longer than they strictly need to.
"There. Now you look like someone who has his life together."
"…Thanks."
We walk on.
"Practice today?"
"Club doesn't start until Wednesday. First week."
"And after that?"
"Monday, Wednesday, Friday, Saturday morning. Shifts Tuesday, Thursday, Sunday."
"I know."
"Then why'd you ask?"
"So you'd hear yourself say it."
"It's fine. Saturday afternoons are free."
"Mm."
A few steps of nothing. The river is loud this time of year, fat with spring rain off the Tanzawa Mountains.
"Oh. Grandpa says the shrine's cherries are the best they've been in years. I'm helping him sweep up there Saturday."
"His back again?"
"His back is a very convenient back. It only hurts on days with a lot of petals."
"I'll come after practice. Somebody has to carry the trash bags while you supervise."
"I do supervise beautifully."
She walks a little faster after that, and for a while I actually have to work to keep up.
The entrance hall is chaos. Two hundred students trying to read six sheets of paper at once.
"Nano-chaaaan!"
A blur with pigtails and a cluster of novelty hair clips hits Nanoha from the side.
"Two-B! You're in Two-B! I'm in Two-B! It's destiny! It's in the stars! I'm making us matching keychains!"
"Good morning, Rika-chan."
Today's clips are a strawberry, a star and a small frog wearing a crown. The frog is new.
"And you walked in with Fujisawa-kun. Hm. Hmmm."
"What's 'hmmm'?"
"Nothing! Nothing! I'm just humming! Hmm-hmm-hmmm!"
"—which is why the correct way to eat a {taiyaki|fish-shaped cake} is head first."
Tokiwa has arrived the way he usually does, in the middle of an argument nobody else knew had started.
"Good morning, Tokiwa."
"The head has the most bean paste. You eat the best part while it's still hot, and the tail cleans your palate. That isn't an opinion. It's thermodynamics."
"It's seven-fifty in the morning."
"Tail first! You save the best part for last! Everybody knows that!"
"Then by the time you get there, it's cold."
"…Oh no."
"We'll resume this at lunch. I'll need a diagram."
"Please don't."
"Oh! Oh oh oh, but have you heard? Two-B is getting a transfer student!"
"A transfer student?"
"A girl! From somewhere! Far!"
"'Somewhere far' covers most of the planet."
"Then we've already narrowed it down!"
While they argue, I squeeze toward the board. I don't make it. Nanoha has already slipped through to the front and is pointing up at a line I can't see yet.
"Fujisawa Kōhei. Two-B. About halfway down."
"You found mine before yours?"
"Yours was easier. It's always right under Fukuda-kun's. Fukuda-kun is easy to find."
When I finally get to the board, Fukuda's not in Two-B this year. He's in Two-E. She went looking for mine before her own.
I don't know why that's the thing that sticks with me all through the opening ceremony.
I end up in the second-to-last row by the window. Nanoha's two rows over, which apparently satisfies the folder. Tokiwa's near the front, already drawing his diagram.
Ōno-sensei, our homeroom teacher, shuffles in with the attendance sheet and the expression of a man who was born in a cardigan.
"All right. Settle down. Before we start—as some of you have apparently already heard, through channels I'd like to know more about—we have a new student joining us this year."
"Come on in."
The door opens.
She walks to the front of a room full of strangers like she's stepping onto a floor she's already won on.
Her hair falls long, in soft waves, brushed until it shines. She smiles at the whole room at once, which shouldn't be possible.
Whispering starts up around the room before she's said a word. "Whoa." "She's so pretty." "Is she an idol or something?" Somebody two rows up leans out into the aisle for a better look.
"I'm Mizuno Natsuki. It's nice to meet you all."
"My dad's job moves us around a lot, so I've been the new girl…"
"…six times now? So please don't go easy on me."
A ripple of laughter. Someone in the front row actually claps.
"I do kendo, and I'm looking for a dojo that'll put up with me. I also love horror movies, the cheesier the better, so if anyone wants to watch a bad one with me, come find me."
Her eyes go along the rows while she says it. Then they get to me.
Her grin stutters. Just for a second. Just long enough that I'm sure I'm the only one who sees it.
"Looking forward to this year."
She bows, and the class gives her the friendly kind of applause.
I realize I've been holding my pen hard enough to hurt.
"Thank you, Mizuno. Let's see… the empty seat behind Fujisawa, by the window. Fujisawa, raise your hand so she doesn't have to wander."
I raise my left hand. She walks down the aisle.
When she passes my desk, she slows down just enough to lean in.
"Hey. Kendo, right?"
"…How did you—"
"Left palm. You've got the callus right where the {tsuka|hilt} sits. It takes years to get it that thick."
I look down at my hand like it's betrayed me.
"Takes one to know one."
And then she's past me, settling into the seat at my back, and I can feel the whole classroom's attention swing toward the window like a weathervane.
I keep my eyes on the board for the entire first period.

By lunch, Mizuno Natsuki has learned the names of half the class, answered "Sendai, most recently" about twenty times, been invited to two clubs, and agreed to go to karaoke with a group of girls whose names I don't think I've ever said out loud.
I've barely gotten the lid off my lunch when a chair scrapes behind me.
"So. You're Fujisawa."
"That's what the attendance sheet says."
"How long have you been doing kendo?"
"Since I was little."
"And you stuck with it. What's the best part?"
Nobody's asked me that before. I answer before I've decided to.
"Having a sword in my hand."
"Just that?"
"I've always been comfortable holding one. Since the first time I picked one up."
I don't say the rest: that with one in my hands, everything else goes quiet for a while.
"Mine's the bow at the start."
"The bow?"
"Six new schools. Every dojo bows the same way."
"Also, you get to yell in a room full of people and nobody calls your parents."
She props her chin on her hand and looks me over. Shoulders. Hands. Like she's working out my reach.
"Do you always sit this straight?"
"What are you, {shodan|first dan}?"
"We'll find out on the floor."
"Big talk for someone who sits like he's being graded."
"Club starts Wednesday."
"Wednesday."
She takes a ballpoint out of her blazer pocket, turns her left hand over and writes {水|Wednesday} on the inside of her wrist, small, just under her cuff.
"Excuse me. Mizuno-san?"
Nanoha's standing by my desk with her lunch held in front of her in both hands, the way she holds things when she's about to do something brave.
"Oh—hi. You're…"
"Tachibana Nanoha. Um— I sit two rows over."
"If you'd like… I could show you around after school? The library, the music rooms. Which shoe lockers stick. Which vending machine eats coins. That kind of thing."
For a second Mizuno doesn't say anything.
"…Really?"
"It's not a big tour. The vending machine part is the most important."
"I'd love that. Which one eats coins?"
"Oh, and call me Natsuki."
"…Natsuki-san."
"Eh, 'san'? We're the same age!"
"I'm working up to it."
"Okay, okay. Then I'll call you Nanoha. All right? I'm doing it anyway."
"That's—yes. That's fine."
Mizuno laughs, and after a second Nanoha does too, ducking her head over her lunch. The two of them in the window light, over the top of my head. I feel like furniture.
I eat my rice. It's good rice. I made it myself.
Natsuki noticed everything.

That was the first thing Nanoha learned on the tour. Natsuki noticed that the stairs by the art room squeaked on the fourth step and the eleventh. She noticed that the third-floor girls' bathroom had a window that looked straight at the mountains, and she said "Oh," softly, like she'd been handed something.
They ended the tour in their own empty classroom, the evening sun coming in sideways and turning every desk gold. Natsuki leaned back against the desk in front of her own.
"Serious question. Is this building haunted? Something in the music room was knocking."
"It's old. The pipes sound like a ghost."
"Perfect."
"So. What about you and Fujisawa?"
"Me and Kōhei?"
"You live next door, right? Somebody said."
"Since we were born."
"No way. Real childhood friends? Baby pictures and everything?"
"Real childhood friends."
Nanoha said it as lightly as she knew how. She'd had practice.
"I've never stayed anywhere long enough to have one of those. You know? Someone who knows which drawer sticks in your kitchen."
Nanoha didn't say that Kōhei's kitchen drawer stuck. She didn't say she'd known it since she was six.
"Hey. Does Fujisawa ever compete up north? Around Sendai?"
"Not that I know of. Why?"
"I feel like I've met him somewhere before. I just can't place it."
"I have met him before. Every day. For sixteen years."
"Ha— okay. Then it's his face. He's got kind of a normal one, right? Don't tell him I said that."
"Thanks for today, Nanoha. Seriously. First days are usually…"
She didn't finish. She just smiled, and it was a different smile from the one she'd used in front of the class. Smaller. It looked like it cost her something.
"Anyway. Thanks."
Somewhere between the library and the gym, Nanoha had decided that she liked Mizuno Natsuki.
She'd decided it firmly, the way you shut a window against the wind.
She did not let herself think about why it had needed deciding at all.
I'm taking the burnables out to the corner. Pickup moved to Tuesdays and Fridays last fall. Dad's handwriting on the whiteboard still says Monday, and tonight I went with the handwriting.
That's when Nanoha comes up the street with her school bag over her shoulder, back from walking Mizuno home to her place by the station.
"You're taking out the trash on the wrong day."
"I'm moving it closer to the right day. How was the tour?"
"Good. She noticed the squeaky stairs. Both of them."
"Nobody notices the eleventh step."
"She did."
"She's nice, Kōhei. I like her."
"What did you think of her?"
"She seems fine."
"You smiled."
"When?"
"When she said she was looking for a dojo that would put up with her. You did your—"
She drops her chin and narrows her eyes. I think it's supposed to be me.
"I don't have a face."
"You have several. I've catalogued them. That one's number four. 'Somebody wants to fight me.'"
"What's number one?"
"Secret."
She walks the ten feet to her own front door. Pauses with her hand on the latch.
"Good night, Kō-chan."
"Night, Chibi."
The door closes.
A moment later her upstairs light comes on, in the window that faces mine across a gap so narrow you could pass a book through it if you leaned.
I stand there for a while longer than the garbage requires.
In bed I run my thumb over the callus on my left palm.
There's a dream I've had since I was small.
I never remember it properly when I wake. Only pieces.
Tonight, it comes back.
The sound of a river, close by.
My wrist stings. There's a cut on the inside of it, where a blade got past me in training, and I've held it closed the whole way home.
Somewhere above us, a branch moving in the wind.
Petals.
"You're late."
She says it like a scolding. She says it like she's laughing.
She says it like she's been waiting a very long time.
"Hurt again. Give me your hand… Hold still."
Hands that aren't mine wind a strip of cloth around a wrist that is. Slow and careful, like the knot matters more than anything else in the world.
And then I wake up, and the only thing left is a feeling I can't put a name to.
That someone was waiting for me.
That I kept them waiting far too long.
Tuesday, April 8
On Tuesday, Mizuno learns the other half of the class's names.
Every so often during class, the back of my neck prickles, the way it does on the floor when someone's measuring the distance between us.
When I turn around, she's always looking at the board.
Tuesday is also a shift. Five-thirty to close at Hoshino Kitchen, the family restaurant by the station: the dish pit, the drink bar, and the register whenever the register needs a body.
"Fujisawa-kun! Table four wants the check, table nine wants water, and the dishwasher's making the noise again!"
"On it."
"Lifesaver!"
That's one. The manager says it about nine times a night.
Akane's dinner is in the fridge at home with a note on the lid. At seven she sends me a photo of the empty container. A minute later she sends a second one, closer up, in case I had questions.
At eight, the automatic door slides open on five girls from Two-B, still in uniform and still loud from karaoke. Mizuno's in the middle of them.
"Nacchan, you have to get the strawberry parfait. Everybody gets the parfait."
"…Fujisawa?"
I'm holding a tray of empty glasses and wearing the Hoshino Kitchen apron, the one with a cartoon chef on the pocket.
"You work here."
"Three nights a week."
"And you tie your apron like a {hakama|pleated kendo trousers}."
I look down. The strings cross in front and finish in a flat knot below my stomach.
"It stays tied."
I put them in the big booth by the window. When I come back with the order tablet, Mizuno has the menu open to the very last page.
"Do you check ID for the kids' plate?"
"Then one kids' plate, please. With the flag."
"Nacchan, you're sixteen!"
"He said they don't check."
She hands me the menu without looking away from me.
I laugh. Right there in the middle of the floor, with the tablet in one hand and her menu in the other.
The kids' plate comes out with a little paper flag stuck in the dome of rice. Mizuno photographs it from three angles before she touches it.
Around eight-forty the girls pile out in a clump, waving at Mizuno through the window.
"Nacchan, aren't you coming?"
"I live right by the station. I'm not done with my flag."
At nine, the manager turns the sign on the door around and decides not to notice the one customer left in the booth.
She talks while I wipe tables. About the town, mostly.
"Is the mountain always that close? From the station it looks like you could walk there."
"It's farther than it looks."
"What about the {taiyaki|fish-shaped cake} stand by the north exit?"
"Red bean's good. Don't get the custard. They burn it."
"Head first or tail first?"
"Don't start."

So I tell her other things instead. Which convenience store has the drink fridge that freezes everything solid. How the river floods the lower path in June, and the herons stand on the bike racks like they're waiting for a train. Where the wind comes down off the mountains strongest, if you want petals in a picture.
She doesn't ask why a second-year works three shifts a week. People usually do, the first time. Then they get careful with me.
When I start putting chairs up on the tables, she gets up without a word and starts on the other side of the room.
"Lifesaver!"
That's nine.
"…Wait. Do you work here?"
"I'm new."
The manager nods like that settles it and goes back to the register.
I laugh so hard I have to put the chair down.
"See you tomorrow, Fujisawa. Wednesday."
She goes out with the little paper flag in her blazer pocket.
I finish the floor. I count out the register. I walk home up the hill.

Somewhere around the bridge I notice my throat's a little rough, and it takes me most of the way home to work out why. I've been talking. For an hour, about {taiyaki||taiyaki} and herons, to someone I met yesterday.
Wednesday, April 9
Wednesday. Two lunch boxes, the eggs, the last of the spinach. Akane is upstairs, losing an argument with her hair.
"Good morning. I'm coming in."
She sets a plastic container on the table.
"Again."
"Morning. Tell your mom thanks."
It comes out rough. I clear my throat.
"You sound like you've been talking."
"I work at a restaurant."
"You work in the dish pit."
She has a point. The dishwasher only makes the one noise.
"Mizuno came in after karaoke, with some girls from class. She stayed till close."
"Mm."
She takes down two mugs without looking and bumps the drawer shut with her hip. Then she turns around and looks at me properly.
"That one's new."
"A new what?"
"Face. I'll have to give it a number."
"What number?"
"I'll tell you when I've decided."
She sets something down next to my lunch box: a throat lozenge, the honey kind, still in its wrapper.
"For the talking."
On the walk to school she's quiet for a while, which isn't unusual, and then for a little longer than that, which is.
Then she asks how many first-years the club is expecting, and we talk about that until the gates.
After school, the dojo smells like it always does in April: old wood, old sweat, and the cedar walls warming up in the sun after a long winter.
Four days a week, for two hours, there's exactly one problem in front of me, and I'm allowed to solve it with my whole body.

Takatsuki is already on the floor when I come in, doing {suburi|practice swings} alone at the far end. Every swing is the same swing: same height, same speed, same snap at the bottom. Watching him is like watching a diagram of kendo.
"Fujisawa."
"Takatsuki."
"Your {hakama|pleated kendo trousers} is tied off center."
"It's the same knot as always."
"Yes. It has been off center for a year."
"Line up."
Kirishima-senpai, the captain, is the only person I know who can quiet a room by not raising his voice. As far as anyone can tell, nothing has ever surprised him.
"Welcome back. One new member, ahead of the first-years: a second-year transfer. Mizuno."
"Mizuno Natsuki, second year. Kendo since I was seven. Who do I get to fight first?"
A couple of the third-years laugh. She looks pleased about it.
"Good."

She's in a faded indigo {keikogi|kendo jacket} and {hakama||hakama}, her hair up in a long ponytail. The {gi||keikogi} has been washed so many times it's gone soft and pale at the seams. Old equipment. Well loved.
"Warm-ups and {suburi||suburi}. {Bogu|armor} after the break."
"Fujisawa. You'll take Mizuno. Find out what she has."
"Captain, I could take her, if—"
"You'll take the first-years when they come, Takatsuki. They'll need someone with patience."
"That was a joke."
Nobody laughs. He seems satisfied anyway.
At the water break after warm-ups, the dojo door slides open a few inches, and Hoshikawa Rika's head comes around it, followed by a sketchbook.
"Nacchan! Art club assignment! 'People in motion'! Can I draw you? Can I sit here? Is this a floor you're allowed to sit on?"
"Shoes off."
"Yes, sir!"
She sits against the wall in her socks with the sketchbook on her knees.
"Okay. Explain everything. All I know is you guys yell."

Two minutes later Mizuno has wiped the practice schedule off the whiteboard by the door, borrowed a pair of glasses from the lost-and-found box, and picked up a {shinai|bamboo practice sword} to point with.
"Whose glasses are those?"
"Lost and found. How do I look?"
"Like a teacher."
"Kendo, lesson one. There are four places you're allowed to hit."
She draws a stick figure on the board. It has an enormous head.
"Men. The head."
"Kote. The wrist. Usually the right one."
"Dō. The side of the body."
"And tsuki, the throat. Thrusts only. You're not allowed to use it until high school."
"We're in high school!"
"So be afraid."
When she steps back, the stick figure has four targets on it, all labeled, and an expression of deep concern.
"How do you get a point? Do you just hit them really hard?"
"{Me-e-en!|Head!|men}"
Her front foot stamps the floor in the same instant, and the {shinai||shinai} stops an inch short of the stick figure's head.
"Hitting isn't enough. Voice, sword and feet, all at once. {Ki-ken-tai-itchi|spirit, sword and body as one}."
"So the yelling is you telling them where."
"That's not why you—"
"And afterward, you stay ready. {Zanshin|remaining mind}. No celebrating. You're still in the fight until somebody tells you you're not."
"Who tells you?"
"The referee. Pop quiz, Rika. I hit Fujisawa on the head. What does the referee say?"
"'Men ari.' There was a head."
"Somebody hits you in the head, and the referee goes, 'There was a head.'"
"What's the hardest one?"
"Debana. You hit them right as they start to attack. It's my favorite."
"How do you know when they're starting?"
"Mostly you don't. That's why it's hard."
"It is the hardest thing in kendo to do on purpose."
"Thank you, Takatsuki-kun. Which brings us to the correct stance. Takatsuki-kun, would you be our model?"
"…If it's educational."
He steps out and settles into {kamae|stance} like a door swinging shut. Left heel just off the floor. Sword tip at the height of an imaginary throat. Not one thing out of place.
"Beautiful. Look at that left heel. And now, for comparison: Fujisawa."
"No."
"The class is waiting."
"Fu-ji-sa-wa! Fu-ji-sa-wa!"
I get up. I don't know why I get up.
I take {kamae||kamae} next to Takatsuki, and Mizuno walks a slow circle around me with the {shinai||shinai}, like a museum guide.
"Left heel, a little low. The tip wanders. He hits {men|head strikes} from the wrong distance and gets away with it, which is the worst possible thing for a first-year to see."
"He's the 'before' picture!"
"Hoshikawa. Don't draw that."
"You're doing great, visual aid."
"Mizuno. For the record, your explanation of {zanshin|staying alert after the strike} was incomplete."
"Incomplete how?"
"Mizuno. The practice schedule was on that board."
"…I'll put it back."
"From memory."
"From memory."

After the break, {bogu|armor}. The {men|helmet} goes on last: the {tenugui|cotton head cloth} tied tight over my hair, the helmet settled down over it, the cords pulled and knotted behind my head. The world narrows to a rectangle behind the grille.
An hour of {kirikaeshi|a drill of nonstop strikes} and {waza|technique} drills later, Kirishima-senpai calls the {shiai-geiko|practice matches}.
Mizuno faces me across the floor. Through the bars of her {men||men} I can see her eyes, and nothing else, and they're bright.
We bow. We step in. We crouch at the line, {shinai|bamboo practice sword} tips crossing.

panels.desc: Page 1, wide (21:9): the two of them crouched at the line, shinai tips crossed; Kirishima standing behind them as referee; club members kneeling along the wall.
Page 1 (16:9): Kōhei, seen past Natsuki's shoulder, lifts his sword tip as if to strike her head. Natsuki hasn't moved at all; her tip stays on his throat.

lines.text: I show her {men|a head strike}. She doesn't even blink.

panels.desc: Page 1, wide (21:9): Kōhei commits, stepping in hard with his arms going up for men. Natsuki's sword is already moving toward his wrist.

lines.text: Half a second, I stop to think. Then I go.

panels.desc: Page 2, large (16:9): her strike lands on his right wrist as his arms come up.
Page 2 (4:3): Kirishima's arm raised toward Natsuki's side.
Page 2 (4:5): close on Kōhei's eyes behind his grille, a bead of sweat.

lines.text: She was there before I moved.

panels.desc: Page 2 (1:1): close on Natsuki behind her grille, laughing, out of breath.
Page 2 (3:2): back at the line, tips crossed again.
Page 3, large (most of the page): Natsuki comes in for his head; Kōhei drops under it as it comes, low, left foot forward (the wrong foot), cutting across her body as they pass.

script.text: We step back to the line. We bow. I'm breathing like I just ran up the shrine stairs twice.
Practice ends the way it starts, with a bow. {Bogu|armor} off, we kneel in a line while Kirishima-senpai walks down it, saying one sentence to each of us.
"Mizuno. Good {kote|wrist strike}. You drop your left shoulder before {men|head strikes}. Fix it."
"Yes, Captain."
"Fujisawa."
"Captain."
"You stopped for half a second. Don't."
"…Yes, Captain."
He moves on down the line. Mizuno leans over before I can get up, her face still flushed from the {men|helmet}.
"You didn't let me have that point, did you?"
"No."
"I know. That's why I'm so happy."
Pure, clean joy at having hit someone on the wrist with a stick. I understand it completely.
"That was {debana-kote|a wrist strike as the attack starts|debana}."
"You did not take his feint, and you were on his wrist the moment he lifted. I have faced Fujisawa for a year. I have never once been there first."
"New-girl luck. It wears off by Friday."
"Luck is not a technique."
She laughs again and finds something on her {hakama|pleated kendo trousers} that needs fixing.
"Also, you laughed inside your {men||men} after the point. That was the part of {zanshin|staying alert after the strike} you left out."
"And Fujisawa. Your left foot was forward on that {dō|body strike}."
"It scored."
"Yes."
Until the first-years join, whoever stays after practice cleans the floor. It's usually me.
Today, Mizuno stays too.
"New member. I'm supposed to do the grunt work, right?"
"First-years are supposed to do the grunt work."
"Then I'm a spiritual first-year. Hand me a rag."

We do the floor the old way: wet {zōkin|floor cloths}, both hands flat on the wood, running bent double down the length of the dojo and back. She's fast at it. She's also, I notice, trying to beat me to the far wall.
"Fujisawa! Race you!"
"It's not a race."
She's already gone.
I go after her. Of course I go after her.

The light has gone long and orange through the high windows. The wet floor shines. Our feet slap on the wood, and she's laughing, and I'm almost laughing, and we hit the far wall at the same moment and turn—
Her heel goes out from under her on the wet floor.
I catch her.
One arm behind her back, my other hand around her forearm. Her weight comes down, and I hold it.
Her face is close. Close enough to see the sweat at her hairline, a strand of hair stuck to her cheek, the moment she breathes in.
I'm aware of exactly where my hand is on her back.
And she's crying.
One tear, sliding from the corner of her eye down her cheek. Her eyes are wide and confused, like she doesn't know where it came from either.
"…Mizuno?"
"Ah—"
She's up and out of my arms in one movement, wiping her face with her sleeve.
"What— ugh, sorry. Sorry. That's so weird."
"Allergies. It's allergies. Cedar pollen. Kanagawa's full of cedar, right?"
"…It's April."
"Late bloomers. They're real. Look it up."
She laughs, too loud, and the laugh goes up into the high ceiling and comes back thin.
I should say something. Make a joke. Let her off the hook.
I can't find one.
"…Thanks for catching me, by the way."
"Yeah. You too. I mean— you're welcome."
"Are your ears always that red?"
She laughs again. It sounds more like her this time.
We finish the floor. We don't race.
Her apartment's by the station. My house is the other way, up toward the hills. The river's where our routes split, so we walk as far as the bridge together.
The streetlights are coming on along the railing, one at a time. The mountains have gone dark blue. Under us, the river's catching the last orange of the sky.
She stops halfway across and takes a picture of it with her phone. Then one of the railing. Then one of a crow on a lamppost, which looks offended.
"I take pictures of every town I live in."
"Why?"
"So I have proof I was there."
She leans her elbows on the railing, over the water.
"Sapporo is four hundred pictures of snow."
A train goes by toward the station, a bright little chain of windows.
"Hey. Fujisawa."
"Mm."
"If you ever want extra practice. Mornings, weekends, whenever. I'm around."
She's looking hard at the river.
"I just mean it was a good match. I haven't had one like that in a long time."
"I work Tuesdays and Thursdays. And Sundays."
"Right. You told me. Forget it, it was a random thought."
It wasn't. She's been carrying it since the dojo, like a cup filled too full.
So I say the only thing I've got.
"Saturday mornings. Club practice. You'll be there?"
"Depends."
"On what?"
"Tell me one thing you do for fun."
I think about it for longer than I'd like her to see.
"…Saturday afternoons are free."
"Doing what?"
"Carrying trash bags up at a shrine."
She looks at me for a long second, like she's waiting for the rest of the joke.
"That's what you do for fun?"
"It's what I do on Saturday afternoons."
"Okay. That's my project, then."
"What is?"
She doesn't answer. She's looking past me, up at the hill, where the Ōzakura is a pale smudge against the dark trees, still holding the last of the light.
"Is that the shrine? With the big tree?"
"That's the Ōzakura."
"I've been wanting to photograph that thing since Monday."
She backs away down the far side of the bridge, still grinning, and waves her whole arm over her head like I'm on the other side of a stadium.
"See you tomorrow, Fujisawa!"
I watch her go until she's gone under the streetlights.
Halfway up the hill, it occurs to me that something's been decided, and I wasn't the one who decided it.
When I get to the house, the light's on in Nanoha's window across the gap.
It's only trash bags.
The apartment was dark when Natsuki let herself in. It usually was.
There was a note on the counter in her mother's handwriting: curry in the fridge, back late, proud of you. Her mother wrote "proud of you" every first week. Natsuki had never asked what for.
Her father was in Yokohama until Friday.

She ate the curry standing up. Then she sat on the floor between the boxes that hadn't been unpacked yet. They said SAPPORO in marker, crossed out, and SENDAI, crossed out, and SHIRASAWA underneath in newer marker.
The little paper flag was still in her blazer pocket from last night. She stood it up in the pen cup on the low table.
Six schools. You learned names fast. You laughed first. You said yes to karaoke. You didn't buy anything that wouldn't fit in a box.
She had a line for it, for when people asked about the moves. She tried it out loud, to see if it still worked.
"I'm amazing at first days. It's the second semesters I never get to."
It still worked. It always got a laugh. It just didn't get one from her.
She took out her phone and opened the chat at the top, the one pinned so long it had its own little gray tab. Chie.
first official kendo practice at the new school 🥋✨🔥
AND??? 👀

oh no
not like that!!! 😤😤 he's good. like scary good 😱⚔️
i knew what he was going to do before he did it. every time
except the last one. didn't see that one at all 🫠
ok that's actually kind of hot
CHIE 😤😤😤
also i cried on him 🙈🙈
NATSUKI
pollen!!!!! 🤧🤧🌸
it's april
why does everyone keep saying that 😩
are you ok tho. for real
Natsuki looked at that last message for a long time.
She didn't know why she'd cried. The fall, probably. First-week nerves.

The match was harder to explain. She'd fought people for nine years; you learned to read shoulders and feet, where the weight went before the sword did, and she'd watched him all through the drills. That should have covered it.
It didn't feel like it covered it, and she didn't like that.

Chie had been her best friend in fourth grade, and again last year, when her dad's work had swung them back through Sendai like a pendulum. Chie was the only person she'd ever managed to keep. Birthday calls. A box of {zunda mochi|sweet green soybean rice cakes} every New Year.
Chie was also more than two hundred miles away.
And there was Nanoha, who had walked her all the way home on Monday without being asked. Natsuki liked her, and not the first-week way, where you like everyone.
Nanoha lived next door to Fujisawa. Natsuki decided that was none of her business, and didn't quite believe herself.
yeah i'm good!! made a friend 🥹 a real one i think. she gave me the tour on monday and showed me the vending machine that eats coins 😂🪙

Natsuki put the phone down and went out onto the little balcony.
The street outside ran along the river under a row of cherry trees, white under the streetlights.
She took eleven pictures. She sent Chie the best one.
The other ten she kept.

notes.karaage: Japanese fried chicken: bite-size pieces marinated in soy sauce, ginger and garlic, dusted in starch and deep-fried. A lunch-box staple, because it's still good cold.
notes.fusuma: A sliding door of thick paper over a wooden frame, used between rooms in a Japanese house.
notes.kinpira: Kinpira gobō: thin strips of burdock root and carrot, stir-fried, then cooked down in soy sauce, sugar and mirin (sweet rice wine). A classic make-ahead side dish that keeps for several days.
notes.taiyaki: A fish-shaped griddle cake (the name means "baked sea bream"), usually filled with sweet red-bean paste and sold hot from street stalls. Whether to start with the head or the tail is an old argument in Japan.
notes.shodan: First dan, the first rank above the beginner grades in kendo, earned at a formal grading exam (kendo has no belts; the rank comes as a certificate). Serious high-school players usually hold first or second dan.
notes.hakama: Wide, pleated trousers worn over the practice jacket in kendo and other traditional martial arts. They're tied with long cords that wrap around the waist and knot at the front.
notes.suburi: Practice swings with the bamboo sword, done in the air, usually dozens or hundreds at a time to warm up and drill clean form.
notes.keikogi: The thick cotton jacket worn for kendo practice, usually dyed indigo. The dye fades with years of washing.
notes.bogu: Kendo armor: the helmet (men), padded gloves (kote), chest protector (dō) and a waist guard (tare).
notes.shinai: The bamboo practice sword used in kendo: four slats of bamboo bound with leather and cord, about the length of a real sword.
notes.men: Two things in kendo: the strike to the top of the head, and the helmet that protects it (a steel grille over the face, padded flaps over the shoulders). As a shout, it names the target as the strike lands.
notes.ki-ken-tai-itchi: "Spirit, sword and body as one": in kendo, a point needs the shout, the strike and the stamp of the front foot to land at the same instant.
notes.zanshin: Literally "remaining mind": staying alert and ready after a strike. In a match, a strike without it doesn't count.
notes.kamae: A kendo stance, especially the basic one with the sword tip held at the opponent's throat.
notes.tenugui: A thin cotton cloth tied over the hair under the kendo helmet, to soak up sweat and keep the helmet snug.
notes.kirikaeshi: A basic kendo drill: a big strike to the head, then a fast run of alternating strikes to the left and right side of the head while stepping forward and back, all at full voice.
notes.waza: Technique. In kendo, waza drills practice specific attacks and counters with a partner.
notes.shiai-geiko: Practice matches: a real kendo match fought in practice, with someone calling the points.
notes.kote: The padded kendo gloves, and the strike to the wrist they protect (usually the right wrist). As a call, "Kote!" names the target as the strike lands.
notes.debana: Striking at the very moment the opponent starts an attack, before it lands. Debana-kote is that strike to the wrist.
notes.dō: The kendo chest protector, and the strike to the side of the body it protects. As a call, "Dō!" names the target as the strike lands.
notes.zōkin: A cleaning rag, usually a folded and stitched towel. Japanese schools clean their own floors, and dojos are wiped down by hand.
notes.zunda mochi: Rice cakes covered in a sweet, bright-green paste of mashed edamame; a specialty of Sendai.
